Into how many cases does the elimination rule made from it split, and what does each case hand back?
level.decl-three.tasks.decl-three-1.intr: The declaration on the board does not meet the requirement. Write a test case for each direction, introduction and use, to find its fault.
level.decl-three.tasks.decl-three-2.afte: The more introduction rules, the easier to introduce and the harder to use: each one more is one more case to handle when taking it apart.
level.decl-three.tasks.decl-three-2.brie: Requirement: “\(A\lor (B\lor C)\)” may be introduced once any one of “A”, “B”, “C” is proved. Following this declaration, fill in whether each case’s conclusion is derivable.
level.decl-three.tasks.decl-three-2.hint: To derive a sentence from “one of three”, each of the three cases must derive it on its own.
level.decl-three.tasks.decl-three-2.intr: The board holds the declaration of “one of three”: three introduction rules, each needing one thing.
level.decl-three.title: Three items
level.decl-true.after: True is often written \mark{top}, the very opposite of \mark{bottom}: knowing it holds tells you nothing more.
level.decl-true.intro.0.t: The opposite of \mark{bottom}: True always holds. The table holds its declaration: one intro rule with no premises, needing nothing.
level.decl-true.tasks.decl-true.brief: Requirement: True needs nothing: it may be introduced whatever is at hand, even with nothing at all. Following this declaration, fill in whether each case’s conclusion is derivable.
level.decl-true.tasks.decl-true.hint.0: This declaration’s elimination rule has one case, which hands back nothing.
level.decl-true.title: Declare True
level.decl-two.after: “Exactly one agrees” cannot be declared, though: an introduction rule can say what makes a sentence, never what stops it.
level.decl-two.intro.0.t: What is declared need not be a connective: whatever holds in ways that can be spelled out can be declared.
level.decl-two.intro.1.t: The declaration of “the motion passes” on the board does not meet the requirement. Write a test case for each direction, introduction and use, to find its fault.
level.decl-two.tasks.decl-two.brief: Requirement: “the motion passes” may be introduced only when at least two of “A”, “B”, “C” are proved. Write two test cases whose expectations meet the requirement and with which this declaration’s results both disagree.
level.decl-two.tasks.decl-two.hint.0: How many pairs can be taken from the three? Which does this declaration write out?
level.decl-two.tasks.decl-two.hint.1: Which sentence is in every one of this declaration’s introduction rules?
level.decl-two.title: Two items
level.demorgan.intro.0.t: “Neither Saturday nor Sunday” and “not (Saturday or Sunday)” say the same; so do “not (Saturday and Sunday)” and “not Saturday, or not Sunday”. These are <wiki-ref to="demorgan"></wiki-ref>.
level.demorgan.tasks.demorgan-1.hint.0: Each half of the goal is a negation.
level.demorgan.tasks.demorgan-1.hint.1: Assume “today is Saturday” and see how it contradicts the given.
level.demorgan.tasks.demorgan-2.hint.1: Assume “\(\text{today is Saturday}\lor \text{today is Sunday}\)” and get a contradiction in each case.
level.demorgan.tasks.demorgan-3.hint.0: The goal is again a negation.
level.demorgan.tasks.demorgan-3.hint.1: Assume “\(\text{today is Saturday}\land \text{today is Sunday}\)”, then take cases on the given.
level.demorgan.tasks.demorgan-4.hint.0: The given does not say which one fails.
level.demorgan.tasks.demorgan-4.hint.1: Today is Saturday, or it is not: take both sides.
level.demorgan.title: De Morgan
level.dist.tasks.dist.hint.0: Split the \mark{and} first, then take cases on the “\(\text{it rains}\lor \text{it’s windy}\)” it gives.
level.dist.tasks.dist.hint.1: In each case, join “today is Saturday” with that case’s assumption, then put it on the matching side of the \mark{or}.
level.dist.title: Distribution
level.drinker.after: It sounds absurd, yet it is a theorem of classical logic: the proof says such a person exists without saying who.
level.drinker.intro.0.t: There is at least one person in the pub. “\(\exists x.\, x\) is drinking \mark{implies} \(\forall y.\, y\) is drinking” says: there is someone such that, if they drink, everyone drinks.
level.drinker.tasks.drinker.hint.0: Do not look for that person yet. Ask first: is everyone drinking?
level.drinker.tasks.drinker.hint.1: If not everyone is drinking, what does <part-ref to="lemma:dm"></part-ref> give?
level.drinker.title: Drinker
level.dsyll.after: This is the <wiki-ref to="dsyll"></wiki-ref>, the logic behind every process of elimination.
level.dsyll.intro.0.t: Bus or bike; not the bus, so the bike.
level.dsyll.tasks.dsyll.hint.0: Take cases. On the “I take the bus” side it runs into “\(\lnot I\; \text{take the bus}\)” and gives \mark{bottom}; from a contradiction, anything.
level.dsyll.title: One ruled out
level.e-count.after: Only one row lights up: a is a knight, b and c are knaves. “At least one” is a string of “or”s; “at most one” is an “or” for every pair, joined by “and”; “not the only one” is a string of “or”s too. Problems such as rostering (at least so many on duty, at most so many on leave at once, someone who may not work alone) are put to a SAT solver the same way: each counting phrase rewritten as strings of “or”s, joined together.
level.e-count.intro.0.t: “At least”, “at most” and “only” speak of how many, and and, or and not have no gate that counts. Such words must first be said another way, as a sentence about whether each person is a knight.
level.e-count.tasks.e-count.brief: a says: “At least one of the three of us is a knave.” b says: “At most one of the three of us is a knave.” c says: “a is not the only knight.” Translate what the three say into logic and wire it: the board outputs true on exactly the rows where what each says fits what they are.
level.e-count.tasks.e-count.hint.0: “At least one is a knave”: of the three, who might that knave be?
level.e-count.tasks.e-count.hint.1: “At most one knave” means no two people are knaves at once. Pick any two people: what must be true of them?
level.e-count.tasks.e-count.hint.2: “a is not the only knight”: either a is not a knight, or there is another knight.
level.e-count.title: Headcount
level.e-one.tasks.e-one.brief: a says: “At least one of us two is a knave.” Translate this into logic and wire it: the board outputs true on exactly the rows where what a says fits what a is.
level.e-one.tasks.e-one.hint.0: Translate what a says first, then “a says”.
level.e-one.tasks.e-one.hint.1: “a is a knave” is “a is not a knight”.
level.e-one.title: One islander
level.e-says.after: Both could be knights, or both could be knaves. This clue leaves two possibilities. In the next puzzles, you’ll use the same method to check more complicated statements.
level.e-says.intro.0.t: You arrive on an island and meet two residents, a and b. Every islander is either a knight, who always tells the truth, or a knave, who always lies.
level.e-says.intro.1.t: a speaks first. Put “a is a knight” and what a says into one formula, then use the truth table to find the identities that fit the island’s rules.
level.e-says.tasks.e-says-translate.brie: Use the cards to express how a’s identity must relate to this clue.
level.e-says.tasks.e-says-translate.hint: If a is a knight, the statement must be true. What if a is a knave?
Which connective requires both sides to have the same truth value?
level.e-says.tasks.e-says.brief: Wire your formula and run the truth table. Find the rows where a’s statement fits a’s identity.
level.e-says.tasks.e-says.hint.0: Use the two knight-status inputs for the two propositions in your formula, then connect them with the corresponding gate.
level.e-says.title: First clue
level.e-three.after: Finding a row on which several sentences are all true is the <wiki-ref to="satisfiable"></wiki-ref> problem (SAT).
level.e-three.intro.0.t: Three people, and the table has eight rows.
level.e-three.tasks.e-three.brief: a says: “b is a knave.” b says: “c is a knave.” c says: “a and b are both knaves.” Translate what the three say into logic and wire it: the board outputs true on exactly the rows where what each says fits what they are.
level.e-three.tasks.e-three.hint.0: In what c says, which part does the negation cover?
level.e-three.tasks.e-three.hint.1: Translate each person’s words on their own; all three must hold at once.
level.e-three.title: Three islanders
level.e-two.tasks.e-two.brief: a says: “b is a knave.” b says: “We are both knights.” Translate what both say into logic and wire it: the board outputs true on exactly the rows where what each says fits what they are.
level.e-two.tasks.e-two.hint.0: Translate what each person says on its own.
level.e-two.title: Two islanders
level.e-words.after: All four rows are false. The rule says rain makes the ground wet, so it can’t hold alongside a report of rain leaving the ground dry. A formula that is false on every row is a <wiki-ref to="contradiction"></wiki-ref>.
level.e-words.intro.0.t: You can wire a simple sentence directly. With a longer sentence, it’s easy to lose track of what each gate should connect. Translate the sentence into a logical formula first, then use the formula to guide your wiring.
level.e-words.intro.1.t: Practice translating a short sentence, then try a more complicated rain report. In the circuit, use the basic claims as inputs and turn the connectives into gates. The truth table runs the circuit once for each combination of inputs.
level.e-words.tasks.e-words-translate.br: The log gives a general rule and describes what just happened. Translate the two claims separately, then use the cards to build one formula that says both hold.
level.e-words.tasks.e-words-translate.hi: Start with “If it rains, the yard gets wet”. Which connective expresses that condition?
The second sentence says it rained and the ground stayed dry. Join the two sentences with another And.
level.e-words.tasks.e-words-translate.sa: The log says: “If it rains, the yard gets wet. It rained, but the yard stayed dry.”
level.e-words.tasks.e-words-warmup.brief: Start with a short sentence. Find its two claims and use the cards to put them into one formula.
The sentence says both that it’s raining and that it’s wet. Which connective requires both claims to be true?
level.e-words.tasks.g-always-2.brief: Wire the formula you just built. Run the truth table and see whether any row makes both claims in the report true.
level.e-words.tasks.g-always-2.hint.0: Revisit Translate the report to check your formula. Wire the inner connectives first, then feed their outputs into the outer ones.
level.e-words.title: Rain report
level.fo-all.after: A sentence that always holds is true in every world, and there are infinitely many worlds, of any size.
level.fo-all.intro.0.t: The universal \mark{forall} reads “for all”: \(\forall x.\, P(x)\) says every thing x in the world satisfies P.
level.fo-all.intro.1.t: First build a sentence as a formula; when it is wrong, the checker may show a small world where it and the target differ. Then someone else has translated the sentence too, and it is your turn to show with a world that they got it wrong.
level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-1.brief: Use the cards to build a formula for this sentence.
level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-1.hint.0: “Every human is mortal”: for every thing x, if x is human then x is mortal.
level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-1.hint.1: Writing “\(x\; \text{is human}\land x\; \text{is mortal}\)” says every thing in the world is human.
level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-2.brief: You built this sentence as a formula; this is someone else’s. Build a world where the two differ in truth.
level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-2.hint.0: Tap a thing to make it human; tap again to undo.
level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-2.hint.1: What does this translation say of every thing? What if the world holds a thing that is not human?
level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-2.intro.0.t: In propositional logic, whether a sentence is true depends on the row of the truth table. In first-order logic it depends on the <wiki-ref to="world"></wiki-ref>: how many things there are, what each is and how they relate.
level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-2.intro.1.t: Above are your translation and someone else’s. To show theirs is wrong, build a world where the two differ: choose below how many things there are, then tap what holds of each. A run marks above whether each translation is true in this world.
level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-3.brief: You built this sentence as a formula; this is someone else’s. Build a world where the two differ in truth.
level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-3.hint.0: A human who is not mortal.
level.fo-all.title: For all
level.fo-atoms.brief: Use the cards to build a formula for this sentence.
level.fo-atoms.intro.0.t: In propositional logic a letter stands for a whole sentence: saying whether each person is mortal takes a letter per person, and “everyone” or “someone” cannot be said at all.
level.fo-atoms.intro.1.t: takes sentences apart: a name stands for a thing, and a says what a thing is or how things relate. “Socrates is human” is written Human(h), “Ann likes Bo” Likes(i, j): the order of the places matters.
level.fo-atoms.intro.2.t: To translate a sentence, find its frame first: the connectives often hide in the wording, “yet” is “and”, “either … or …” is “or”, “only if” is “if … then …” with the condition at the end. No proofs in this chapter yet: first how to say a sentence, and how to tell whether it is true in a world.
level.fo-atoms.tasks.fo-atoms-1.hint.0: “Yet”, “but” and “and” are all \mark{and} in logic: both halves hold.
level.fo-atoms.tasks.fo-atoms-1.hint.1: In “\mark{circle-1} is a parent of \mark{circle-2}”, who is \mark{circle-1}, who is \mark{circle-2}? The \mark{not} covers only the second half.
level.fo-atoms.tasks.fo-atoms-1.say: Ann is a parent of Bo, yet Bo does not like Ann.
level.fo-atoms.tasks.fo-atoms-2.hint.0: “Either … or …” has no “not” in it: at least one of the two holds, so it is \mark{or}.
level.fo-atoms.tasks.fo-atoms-2.say: Socrates is either a bird or human.
level.fo-atoms.tasks.fo-atoms-3.hint.0: “Only if A, B” says: if B holds, A must hold. The condition is the second half.
level.fo-atoms.tasks.fo-atoms-3.say: Ann likes Bo only if Bo is human.
level.fo-atoms.title: Translation
level.fo-nested.intro.0.t: A quantifier may hold another. Each has its own variable and reaches over everything after it: in \(\forall x\). … \(\exists y\). …, x and y each stand for their own thing. A variable some quantifier covers is a <wiki-ref to="bound"></wiki-ref>; one no quantifier covers is a <wiki-ref to="free"></wiki-ref>, and then the sentence does not say whom it means.
level.fo-nested.tasks.fo-nested-1.brief: Use the cards to build a formula for this sentence.
level.fo-nested.tasks.fo-nested-1.hint.0: Outside, every x; inside, some y: the thing x likes takes another variable.
level.fo-nested.tasks.fo-nested-2.brief: Use the cards to build a formula for this sentence.
level.fo-nested.tasks.fo-nested-2.hint.0: For every x, if x is human, then some y is a parent of x.
level.fo-nested.tasks.fo-nested-3.brief: Someone else translated the first sentence too. Build a world where their formula and yours differ in truth.
level.fo-nested.tasks.fo-nested-3.hint.0: Think of it as a game: the opponent picks for \mark{forall}, you pick for \mark{exists}. In the first, the opponent picks x first, then you pick y; in the second you pick y first, then the opponent picks x.
level.fo-nested.title: Nested scope
level.fo-some.intro.0.t: A new symbol, \mark{exists}, reads “there exists”: \(\exists x.\, P(x)\) says at least one thing x in the world satisfies P.
level.fo-some.intro.1.t: First build a sentence as a formula; when it is wrong, the checker may show a small world where it and the target differ. Then someone else has translated the sentence too, and it is your turn to show with a world that they got it wrong.
level.fo-some.tasks.fo-some-1.brief: Use the cards to build a formula for this sentence.
level.fo-some.tasks.fo-some-1.hint.0: “Some bird flies”: there is a thing x that is a bird and flies.
level.fo-some.tasks.fo-some-1.hint.1: Writing “\(x\; \text{is a bird}\to x\; \text{flies}\)” is made true by anything at all that is not a bird.
level.fo-some.tasks.fo-some-2.brief: You built this sentence as a formula; this is someone else’s. Build a world where the two differ in truth.
level.fo-some.tasks.fo-some-2.hint.0: What if the world holds no bird at all?
level.fo-some.tasks.fo-some-2.intro.0.t: In propositional logic, whether a sentence is true depends on the row of the truth table. In first-order logic it depends on the world: how many things there are, what each is and how they relate.
level.fo-some.tasks.fo-some-2.intro.1.t: Above are your translation and someone else’s. To show theirs is wrong, build a world where the two differ: choose below how many things there are, then tap what holds of each. A run marks above whether each translation is true in this world.
level.fo-some.title: There exists
level.g-always.after: The first sentence is true on every row: it is a <wiki-ref to="tautology"></wiki-ref>. Its negation is false on every row: it is a <wiki-ref to="contradiction"></wiki-ref>. Their truth values match \mark{top} and \mark{bottom}, respectively. Both circuits are now available as Always True and Contradiction parts.
level.g-always.intro.0.t: An Implies gate has a direction. If you join the two directions with Or, which rows can come out false?
level.g-always.tasks.g-always-1.brief: Wire a circuit to find the truth value of “‘if it rains, it’s wet’ or ‘if it’s wet, it rains’” on every row.
level.g-always.tasks.g-always-1.hint.0: Wire “it rains” and “it’s wet” into the two Implies gates in opposite orders.
level.g-always.tasks.g-always-false.brie: Wire a circuit to evaluate the claim that the previous statement does not hold. Run it and inspect every row.
level.g-always.tasks.g-always-false.hint: The Always True part you just built gives the original statement’s value. How can you say it does not hold?
level.g-always.tasks.g-always-false.intr: The previous statement holds on every row. What happens if we say it does not hold?
level.g-always.title: True and false
level.g-and.intro.0.t: A truth table is filled in row by row. Wire a circuit once and the machine runs it on every row. Select a row to see each part’s value.
level.g-and.intro.1.t: The new part <part-ref to="part:gAnd"></part-ref> outputs true only when both inputs are true.
level.g-and.tasks.g-and.brief: Wire a circuit to find the truth value of “It rains and it is windy” on every row.
level.g-and.tasks.g-and.hint.0: The sentence holds only when both rain and wind are present.
level.g-and.title: And
level.g-iff.after: When both directions hold, the inputs have matching truth values. This is <wiki-ref to="equivalence"></wiki-ref>, written \mark{iff}. The circuit you built is now available as the “Equivalent” gate.
level.g-iff.intro.0.t: Earlier, Or required at least one direction to hold. Now use And to require both directions and see what happens to the output.
level.g-iff.tasks.g-iff.brief: Wire a circuit to find the truth value of “‘if it rains, it’s wet’ and ‘if it’s wet, it rains’” on every row.
level.g-iff.tasks.g-iff.hint.0: Compare the two input columns. Find the rows where their values match.
level.g-iff.title: Equivalence
level.g-imp.after: With the condition and result swapped, the new claim is false only when it’s wet and it didn’t rain. Input order matters for an Implies gate.
level.g-imp.intro.0.t: Remember the forecast in <level-ref to="table"></level-ref>? “If it rains, it’s wet” is false only when it rains and the ground stays dry. The conditional is true whenever it doesn’t rain or it’s wet.
level.g-imp.tasks.g-imp-2.brief: Wire a circuit to find the truth value of “if it’s wet, it must have rained” on every row.
level.g-imp.tasks.g-imp-2.hint.0: Wire the condition that follows “if” into the first input of the Implies gate.
level.g-imp.tasks.g-imp.brief: Wire a circuit to find the truth value of “it isn’t raining or it’s wet” on every row.
level.g-imp.tasks.g-imp.hint.0: Wire “it’s wet” straight into Or. Only “it rains” goes through Not first.
level.g-imp.title: Implies
level.g-not.intro.0.t: A truth table is filled in row by row. A <wiki-ref to="logic/circuit"></wiki-ref> is wired once, and the machine runs it on every row.
level.g-not.intro.1.t: “It rains” on the left gives its value on the current row; “The sentence” on the right takes the board’s output.
level.g-not.intro.2.t: The new part stands for negation, \mark{not}: true in gives false out, false in gives true out.
level.g-not.intro.3.t: Select a row of the truth table to see each part’s value on that row.
level.g-not.tasks.g-not.brief: Wire a board that works out the value of “it is not the case that it is not raining” on every row.
level.g-not.tasks.g-not.hint.0: How is “it is not raining” wired? And negated once more?
level.g-not.title: Not
level.g-or.after: Or needs at least one true input. The gate still outputs true when it’s both raining and windy.
level.g-or.intro.0.t: “It rains or it’s wet” is false only when there’s no rain and the ground is dry. Build that behavior with the gates you have, then pack the circuit into an Or gate.
level.g-or.tasks.g-or-2.brief: Wire a circuit to find the truth value of “it’s raining or it’s windy” on every row.
level.g-or.tasks.g-or.brief: Wire a circuit to find the truth value of “it’s not the case that ‘it isn’t raining and the ground is dry’” on every row.
level.g-or.tasks.g-or.hint.0: Feed the And output into the last Not gate, then wire its output to “The sentence”.
level.g-or.title: Or
level.g-tree.after: “It is windy but not raining” requires wind and no rain. “Rain and wind did not occur together” rules out only their occurring together. The scope of the negation changes the truth value.
level.g-tree.intro.0.t: A sentence can deny one thing, or deny that two things happen together. Wire each sentence and compare their truth tables.
level.g-tree.tasks.g-tree-together.brief: Wire a circuit to find the truth value of “Rain and wind did not occur together” on every row. Compare the two truth tables.
Which combination of rain and wind does this sentence rule out?
level.g-tree.tasks.g-tree.brief: Wire a circuit to find the truth value of “It is windy but not raining” on every row.
level.g-tree.tasks.g-tree.hint.0: What does the sentence say about rain and about wind?
level.g-tree.title: Scope
level.g-xor.tasks.g-xor.brief: “Either it rains or it’s windy, but not both.” Wire a board that computes it, with at most 4 gates.
level.g-xor.tasks.g-xor.hint.0: No need to part it together row by row. Read the sentence as it is said: what parts is it made of?
level.g-xor.title: XOR
level.h-and-make.after: R may be any sentence, even the very “A and B” being defined. Only because that is allowed can the definition be written at all. Isabelle/HOL takes this road: “and” and “or” are not declared but defined this way, with \mark{implies} and \mark{forall}, and their rules proved from the definitions.
level.h-and-make.intro.0.t: <level-ref to="decl-and"></level-ref> brought “and” into the kernel by a declaration. Another way declares nothing and uses the \mark{implies} and quantifier already there: “A and B” is “for every sentence R, if R follows from A and B, then R”, written \mark{forall}R. \((A\to (B\to R))\to R\).
level.h-and-make.intro.1.t: This \mark{forall} ranges not over things but over sentences. The same two parts handle it: take the upper-case name R in the <part-ref to="part:allI"></part-ref>, and inside it R is any sentence at all; in <part-ref to="part:allE"></part-ref> choose not a thing but a sentence, to put in for R.
level.h-and-make.tasks.h-and-make-1.hint: The goal must hold for every sentence R: start with a for-any box, taking the name R.
Inside, the goal is an “if … then …”: assume “\(A\to (B\to R)\)” and Apply twice.
level.h-and-make.tasks.h-and-make-2.hint: Choose an instance: put “A” in for R, to get “\((A\to (B\to A))\to A\)”.
To apply it, “\(A\to (B\to A)\)” is missing: <part-ref to="lemma:axK"></part-ref> gives it.
level.h-and-make.tasks.h-and-make-2.intr: The definition holds for every sentence R, so pick one that serves: R may be A itself.
level.h-and-make.title: Define And
level.h-eq-refl.after: The reflexivity a declaration gives is, under the definition, a conclusion proved.
level.h-eq-refl.intro.0.t: <level-ref to="decl-eq"></level-ref> declared equality into the kernel. It can also be defined with a quantifier instead: “a = b” is “every property a has, b has”, written \mark{forall}P. \(P(a)\to P(b)\).
level.h-eq-refl.intro.1.t: This \mark{forall} ranges over properties: P(x) is a sentence about x. The <part-ref to="part:allI"></part-ref> takes the upper-case P. By this definition, the Morning Star = the Morning Star is this level’s goal.
level.h-eq-refl.tasks.h-eq-refl.brief: From nothing, prove: for every property, if the Morning Star has that property, then the Morning Star has it.
level.h-eq-refl.tasks.h-eq-refl.hint.0: Take the name P in the for-any box: inside, P is any property at all.
level.h-eq-refl.tasks.h-eq-refl.hint.1: Inside goes an assumption box whose assumption is just the conclusion it wants.
level.h-eq-refl.title: Self equality
level.h-eq-subst.after: This is <part-ref to="part:rewrite"></part-ref>: the definition writes down equality’s elimination rule directly.
level.h-eq-subst.intro.0.t: Given the Morning Star = the Evening Star, written out by the definition. <part-ref to="part:allE"></part-ref> puts in a sentence about x for P: each P(t) becomes that sentence with t in place of x.
level.h-eq-subst.tasks.h-eq-subst.hint.0: In <part-ref to="part:allE"></part-ref> choose a property: “B(x)”, to put in for P.
level.h-eq-subst.tasks.h-eq-subst.hint.1: That gives “\(B(\text{the Morning Star})\to B(\text{the Evening Star})\)”; then Apply.
level.h-eq-subst.title: Substitution
level.h-eq-sym.after: With equality declared, symmetry is proved from reflexivity and substitution; with it defined, reflexivity and substitution come from the definition, and symmetry with them. Both ways give the same rules.
level.h-eq-sym.intro.0.t: The definition says one direction only: what the Morning Star has, the Evening Star has. The other way holds too, with a well-chosen property.
level.h-eq-sym.tasks.h-eq-sym.brief: Given the Morning Star = the Evening Star (by the definition), prove the Evening Star = the Morning Star (by the definition too).
level.h-eq-sym.tasks.h-eq-sym.hint.0: A for-any box takes Q. Inside, choose an instance of the given with the property “\(Q(x)\to Q(\text{the Morning Star})\)”.
level.h-eq-sym.tasks.h-eq-sym.hint.1: That gives “\((Q(\text{the Morning Star})\to Q(\text{the Morning Star}))\to (Q(\text{the Evening Star})\to Q(\text{the Morning Star}))\)”: the first half is what <level-ref to="h-eq-refl"></level-ref> proved; give it with an assumption box, then Apply.
level.h-eq-sym.title: Both ways
level.h-or-make.after: A declaration gives the intro rules and the elimination rule is made from them; a definition like this writes down the elimination rule, and the intro rules are proved from it. Both roads give the same rules.
level.h-or-make.intro.0.t: “Or” can be defined the same way: “A or B” is “for every sentence R, if R follows from A and R follows from B, then R”, written \mark{forall}R. \((A\to R)\to ((B\to R)\to R)\).
level.h-or-make.tasks.h-or-make-1.hint.0: A for-any box takes R; inside, the goal has two layers of “if … then …”.
level.h-or-make.tasks.h-or-make-2.hint.0: The conclusion wanted is C: put C in for R, then hand it the two moves in turn.
level.h-or-make.title: Define Or
level.iffUse.after: Eq. substitution leaves the rest of the proved sentence in place. Next, you will use the same rule to rewrite a goal on the machine board.
level.iffUse.intro.0.t: In the truth circuits, the \mark{iff} of <level-ref to="g-iff"></level-ref> meant true together and false together. In the kernel, \(A\leftrightarrow B\) is “\((A\to B)\land (B\to A)\)”: the \mark{implies} holds both ways.
level.iffUse.tasks.iffUse-1.hint.0: <part-ref to="part:andE"></part-ref> splits \mark{iff} too: into the two “if … then …”s; use the right one.
level.iffUse.tasks.iffUse-2.hint.0: This time it takes the other direction: assume “I rest” and see whether it runs into a contradiction.
level.iffUse.tasks.iffUse-subst.brief: Use Eq. substitution to replace \(A\) in \(\neg A\) with \(B\) and prove \(\neg B\).
level.iffUse.tasks.iffUse-subst.hint.0: Connect \(A\leftrightarrow B\) to Equivalence and \(\neg A\) to Original sentence. Then select the boxed \(A\) in the original sentence.
You just proved \(
eg B\) from \(
eg A\) in several steps. Now connect the equivalence and \(
eg A\) to the substitution card and see what changes when you replace the inner \(A\).
level.iffUse.title: Equivalence
level.is-silent.intro.0.t: a says “b is a knave”. b stays silent. c says “a and b are the same kind”.
level.is-silent.tasks.is-silent.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves the identities it can determine and reports failure for the rest.
level.is-silent.tasks.is-silent.hint.0: Not everyone’s kind can be settled.
level.is-silent.title: Missing facts
level.is-ten.after: The truth table for ten people has 1024 rows. Programs that decide problems like this are called SAT solvers, and they handle millions of variables.
level.is-ten.intro.0.t: Ten people stand in a ring. From a to i, each says the next person is a knave. j says “a and b are both knaves”.
level.is-ten.tasks.is-ten.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.is-ten.tasks.is-ten.hint.0: The proof assistant need not change.
level.is-ten.tasks.is-ten.inputs.0.label: Goal
level.is-ten.title: Ten islanders
level.is-three.intro.0.t: a says “b is a knave”, b says “c is a knave”, and c says “a and b are both knaves”.
level.is-three.intro.1.t: These three were wired as a circuit and run on all eight rows in <level-ref to="e-three"></level-ref>, and proved by hand in <level-ref to="kk-three"></level-ref>. This time, hand them to the proof assistant.

level.machine-rewrite-join.after: Both goals left by backward Join must be proved. Each time a goal closes, the next one becomes current.

level.machine-rewrite.after: The rewrite replaced one matching occurrence. The givens and the rest of the goal stayed the same.

level.nested.intro.1.t: The parentheses show which parts belong together. One use of Apply can produce an entire conditional, which can then serve as a premise in further reasoning, just like a given.

level.r-rule.intro.0.t: On the proof board a proof is wired downwards from the givens. A proof assistant works the other way, from the goal back: <wiki-ref to="backward"></wiki-ref>. A new part, <part-ref to="part:rule"></part-ref>: wire a rule into its port “R”; it fits the first goal to the rule’s conclusion and replaces that goal with the rule’s premises, one new goal for each. Every proof-board part is, on this board, a part that gives its rule, and several rule parts can be chained into one list.
level.r-rule.intro.1.t: Recall the assumption box rule “\(\llbracket \llbracket A\rrbracket \Longrightarrow B\rrbracket \Longrightarrow A\to B\)”. Its conclusion matches an “if” goal. When a rule is used backwards, its letters are not yet settled and are written ?A and ?B. Used backwards, this rule replaces that goal with “assume ?A and prove ?B”. The wires carry a <wiki-ref to="proof-state"></wiki-ref>, the goals that remain to be proved.

level.s-repeat.intro.0.t: So far a proof assistant’s parts have run in a fixed order, fit for goals of one structure; change the nesting and it must be rewired. A program that chooses and combines steps by the proof state is a <wiki-ref to="tactic"></wiki-ref>. Isabelle’s auto and Lean’s simp are tactics.

level.s-search.after: This is a simple proof assistant: three kinds of step and a backtracking search. Every proof it finds uses only the kernel’s rules, so it is just as trustworthy. There is also what it cannot do: when a given has another “if” inside it (like “\(\text{it rains}\to (\text{it’s windy}\to \text{it’s wet})\)”, which Swap needs), Apply used backwards once does not reach the goal. And it only knows “if … then …”: next the kernel learns new connectives, and the proof assistant will learn to use them too.
level.s-search.intro.0.t: Givens lead into givens: how many times Apply is used backwards, and which given each time, is not known beforehand. The repeat frame follows only the first result, and stops in a dead end.

level.s-try.tasks.s-try.hint.0: Some goals need a given taken apart, some do not.
level.s-try.tasks.s-try.hint.1: Use the result of unpacking the given as the first route. The second route can carry the state through unchanged.
level.s-try.tasks.s-try.inputs.0.label: Goal
level.s-try.title: Try
level.s.intro.0.t: When it rains, if it’s windy it’s wet; when it rains, it’s windy. So when it rains, it’s wet: Apply under the condition “it rains”. This sentence is called <part-ref to="lemma:axS"></part-ref>.
level.s.tasks.s.hint.1: Inside the innermost box, all three assumptions are visible.
level.s.title: Conditional use
level.sp-back.intro.0.t: A rewrite rule works only left to right: \(\lnot (A\lor B)\longmapsto \lnot A\land \lnot B\) pushes a negation in, but cannot bring it out.
level.sp-back.tasks.sp-back.brief: Design a proof assistant that makes the two negations in each goal one, outside the brackets.
level.sp-back.tasks.sp-back.hint.0: <part-ref to="lemma:dm"></part-ref> still has shapes you have not used.
level.sp-back.title: Direction
level.sp-cnf.after: Automatic provers usually bring a sentence to conjunctive normal form before anything else.
level.sp-cnf.intro.0.t: <wiki-ref to="cnf"></wiki-ref>: negation normal form, with every “or” under the “and”s, a few strings of “or” joined by “and”. Each string of “or” is a <wiki-ref to="clause"></wiki-ref>.
level.sp-cnf.tasks.sp-cnf.brief: Design a proof assistant that transforms each goal into the required form.
level.sp-cnf.tasks.sp-cnf.hint.1: What is left is to bring every “or” under the “and”s.
level.sp-cnf.tasks.sp-cnf.inputs.0.label: Goal
level.sp-cnf.title: Clause form
level.sp-dm.intro.0.t: <part-ref to="lemma:dm"></part-ref> has eight shapes, and each can serve as a rewrite rule.
level.sp-dm.tasks.sp-dm-1.brief: Design a proof assistant that pushes the negation in each goal inside the brackets.
level.sp-dm.tasks.sp-dm-1.hint.1: One rewrite rule fits only one shape; to try both, see <part-ref to="part:append"></part-ref>.
level.sp-dm.tasks.sp-dm-1.inputs.0.label: Goal
level.sp-dm.tasks.sp-dm-2.brief: Design a proof assistant that pushes the negation in each goal past the quantifier.
level.sp-dm.tasks.sp-dm-2.inputs.0.label: Goal
level.sp-dm.title: Negation
level.sp-laws.intro.0.t: <part-ref to="lemma:arrow"></part-ref> and <part-ref to="lemma:dist"></part-ref> are equivalences proved both ways too.
level.sp-laws.tasks.sp-laws-1.brief: Design a proof assistant that turns the “if … then …” in each goal into an “or”.
level.sp-laws.tasks.sp-laws-1.hint.0: Look at the two shapes of <part-ref to="lemma:arrow"></part-ref>.
level.sp-laws.tasks.sp-laws-2.brief: Design a proof assistant that distributes the “or” in each goal over the “and”.
level.sp-laws.tasks.sp-laws-2.hint.0: In one goal the “and” is on the right, in the other on the left.
level.sp-laws.tasks.sp-laws-2.hint.1: One rewrite rule fits only one shape; to try both, see <part-ref to="part:append"></part-ref>.
level.sp-laws.title: Rewrite rules
level.sp-nnf.intro.0.t: <wiki-ref to="nnf"></wiki-ref>: no \mark{implies} in the sentence, and every \mark{not} on a smallest sentence.
level.sp-nnf.tasks.sp-nnf.brief: Design a proof assistant that transforms each goal into the required form.
level.sp-nnf.tasks.sp-nnf.hint.1: Then see in front of which connectives and quantifiers a \mark{not} can stand.
level.sp-nnf.tasks.sp-nnf.inputs.0.label: Goal
level.sp-nnf.title: Normal form
level.sp-order.intro.0.t: Each time, Simp uses the first rule in the list that fits. The same rules in a different order can give a different sentence.
level.sp-order.tasks.sp-order.brief: Design a proof assistant that brings each goal to its shortest conjunctive normal form.
level.sp-order.tasks.sp-order.hint.0: What happens if you distribute while a negation is still outside?
level.sp-order.title: Rule order
level.sp-repeat.intro.0.t: This time the goals hold different numbers of \(\lnot \lnot s\). A rewrite that fits nowhere fails.
level.sp-repeat.tasks.sp-repeat.brief: Design a proof assistant that transforms each goal into the required form.
level.sp-repeat.tasks.sp-repeat.hint.0: The number of rewrites must depend on the goal.
level.sp-repeat.title: Repetition
level.sp-rw.after: This is the basic move of a <wiki-ref to="simplifier"></wiki-ref>.
level.sp-rw.intro.0.t: To turn the \mark{not}\mark{not}it rains in “it’s windy \mark{and} \mark{not}\mark{not}it rains” into it rains, the proof board must take the outer “and” apart, replace the part inside, and put it back together.
level.sp-rw.intro.1.t: Where two sentences are equivalent, one can be swapped for the other right inside a sentence. An equivalence used this way is a <wiki-ref to="rewrite"></wiki-ref>; the new part <part-ref to="part:rw"></part-ref> uses one to change one place in the goal.
level.sp-rw.tasks.sp-rw.brief: Design a proof assistant that takes the \mark{not}\mark{not} out of each goal.
level.sp-rw.tasks.sp-rw.hint.0: Both shapes of <part-ref to="lemma:dneg"></part-ref> can serve as rewrite rules.
level.sp-rw.tasks.sp-rw.inputs.0.label: Goal
level.sp-rw.title: Rewrite
level.sp-simp.after: This is what simp does in Isabelle and Lean too.
level.sp-simp.intro.0.t: Several rewrite rules used together, each time whichever fits, until none fits: this is simplification. The rules come in at the board’s input Rules; the proof assistant you design becomes a new part, , and that input becomes its port Rules.
level.sp-simp.tasks.sp-simp.brief: Design a proof assistant that rewrites each goal with the rules from the input Rules until none of them fits.
level.sp-simp.tasks.sp-simp.hint.0: As in <level-ref to="sp-repeat"></level-ref>, the rewriting goes on until nothing fits.
level.sp-simp.tasks.sp-simp.hint.1: <part-ref to="part:rw"></part-ref> can take a list of rules too, and uses the first that fits.
level.sp-simp.title: Many rules
level.sp-where.intro.0.t: <part-ref to="part:rw"></part-ref> changes one place. When more than one place fits, it changes the first, going outside in and left to right.
level.sp-where.tasks.sp-where.brief: Design a proof assistant that transforms each goal into the required form.
level.sp-where.title: Matching
level.swap.intro.0.t: “On a Saturday, if it rains I rest” and “if it rains, on a Saturday I rest” say the same thing, but the kernel only accepts what is proved.
level.swap.tasks.swap.hint.0: How many \mark{implies}s are in the goal?
level.swap.tasks.swap.hint.1: Inside the innermost box, both conditions are visible.
level.swap.title: Order
level.table.after: The forecast is false only if it rains and the ground stays dry. This reading of “if … then …” is called material implication.
level.table.intro.0.t: The forecast says, “If it rains, then it’s wet.” This statement can be true or false, so it is a proposition.
level.table.intro.1.t: “It rains” and “it’s wet” can each be true or false, giving four combinations. A <wiki-ref to="truth"></wiki-ref> records one combination per row and shows whether the whole forecast is true in that case.
level.table.intro.2.t: In “if X, then Y”, X is the antecedent and Y is the consequent. Here, “it rains” is the antecedent and “it’s wet” is the consequent.
level.table.tasks.table.brief: Use the rain and ground conditions in each row to mark “If it rains, then it’s wet” as true or false.
level.table.tasks.table.hint.0: In which case has the forecast got it wrong?
level.table.tasks.table.hint.1: On the two rows where it does not rain, has the forecast got it wrong?
level.table.title: Truth table
level.try-backtracking.after: A rule can apply even when the resulting goal cannot be proved. Join candidates preserves the other route, so Backtracking can return to it if the first route fails.
level.try-backtracking.intro.0.t: To prove “if it rains, it’s wet”, you can use an assumption box: add “it rains” to the givens, then try to prove “it’s wet”. If the full conditional is already a given, you can cite it directly.
level.try-backtracking.intro.1.t: Use Join candidates to send both routes to Backtracking. Try ① first. If it reaches a dead end, return to the fork and try ②. Switch the run report to the branch tree to see which path finishes the proof.
level.try-backtracking.tasks.try-backtra: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
Wire Input and Expected to the outside of the box. Inside, wire Each step to both backward cards, then connect Assume to ① and Cite a given to ②. Wire the join to the box’s inner result port.
level.try-backtracking.title: Backtracking
level.try-direct-backward.after: Each \mark{backward} card applies a proof rule directly to the current goal. Its output can feed the next tactic card.
level.try-direct-backward.intro.0.t: A card marked \mark{backward} takes a proof state directly. \mark{backward} Assume adds the condition of an implication to the givens. \mark{backward} Cite a given closes a goal that matches a given.
level.try-direct-backward.tasks.try-dire: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
Start with \mark{backward} Assume, then finish with \mark{backward} Cite a given.
level.try-direct-backward.title: Backward rules
level.try-direct-rewrite.after: The double-negation law can rewrite inside a formula. In these cases it removes the double negation and leaves the surrounding formula intact.
level.try-direct-rewrite.intro.0.t: A card marked \mark{rewrite} rewrites a proof state directly. Pick a direction on \mark{rewrite} Double negation and see how it rewrites one part of a larger formula.
level.try-direct-rewrite.tasks.try-direc: Design a proof assistant that uses a rewrite card to remove the double negation in each goal.
Choose the rule that turns \(\lnot \lnot A\) into A.
level.try-direct-rewrite.title: Rewrite
level.try-or-elim.after: The elimination rule is \(\llbracket A\lor B;\ \llbracket A\rrbracket\Longrightarrow R;\ \llbracket B\rrbracket\Longrightarrow R\rrbracket\Longrightarrow R\). When the introduction rules describe all the ways to construct a proof, a case analysis rule can be generated from them. Each introduction rule gives one branch. Both branches reach the same R, so \(A\lor B\) is enough to use that case analysis.
level.try-or-elim.intro.0.t: Suppose a classmate will take the bus or the train. To show they can arrive by eight, consider each route. The same idea works for \(A\lor B\). To use it, consider the case where A holds and the case where B holds.
level.try-or-elim.intro.1.t: Or has two introduction rules. A proof of A gives \(A\lor B\), and so does a proof of B.
level.try-or-elim.tasks.try-or-elim.brie: R stands for any proposition. The premise \(A\lor B\) and conclusion R are fixed. Add two premises using the “assume … and derive …” card to show how each case leads to R.
level.try-or-elim.tasks.try-or-elim.hint: Assume A on one card and B on the other. Both cards must derive R.
level.try-or-elim.title: Or rule
level.try-rule-box.after: The correct rule is \(\llbracket\llbracket A\rrbracket\Longrightarrow B\rrbracket\Longrightarrow A\to B\). Its input is a derivation of B under assumption A, so it also works when B depends on A.
level.try-rule-box.intro.0.t: Someone wrote the assumption-box rule as \(\llbracket B\rrbracket\Longrightarrow A\to B\). Use a test case to see whether it accepts the input you normally give the box.
level.try-rule-box.intro.1.t: A test case lists the input evidence, the conclusion you want, and the expected result. \(\llbracket A\rrbracket\Longrightarrow B\) means “assume A and derive B under that assumption.”
level.try-rule-box.tasks.try-rule-box.br: Edit the test case’s premise to give the assumption box an input it should accept. Run the test to find what the rule overlooks.
level.try-rule-box.tasks.try-rule-box.hi: Replace B with a derivation of B under A. Use the \(\llbracket\Box\rrbracket\Longrightarrow\Box\) card and fill in A and B.
level.try-rule-box.title: Rule check
level.try-rules.after: Apply takes a conditional and its condition to give its result. Chain combines two conditionals into one, ready for the next step.
level.try-rules.intro.0.t: Inputs take premises and the output gives the conclusion. A rule is written \(\llbracket\text{premises}\rrbracket\Longrightarrow\text{conclusion}\). A, B, and C can stand for any propositions. Each letter keeps the same meaning within a rule.
level.try-rules.intro.1.t: Select “Add a premise” for each input. Select the empty slot in “Conclusion” to enter the output, then select “Check”.
level.try-rules.tasks.try-rules-apply.br: Write the premises and conclusion of <part-ref to="part:mp"></part-ref> on the rule board.
level.try-rules.tasks.try-rules-apply.hi: The two inputs take \(A\to B\) and A. Which sentence comes out?
level.try-rules.tasks.try-rules-chain.br: Feed \(A\to B\) and \(B\to C\) into <part-ref to="lemma:chain"></part-ref>. Write its premises and conclusion on the rule board.
level.try-rules.tasks.try-rules-chain.hi: Start at A and go through B. What do you reach? Write the implication from start to finish.
level.try-rules.title: Rules
level.twice.intro.0.t: “\(\text{it rains}\to (\text{it rains}\to \text{it’s wet})\)” states the condition “it rains” twice. Surely once is enough.
level.twice.tasks.twice.hint.0: The goal is “if it rains, then …”.
level.twice.tasks.twice.hint.1: How many times can an assumption in a box be used?
level.twice.title: Repeated premise
level.u-barber.after: This kind of argument is the <wiki-ref to="diagonal"></wiki-ref>.
level.u-barber.intro.0.t: When a goal follows, the saturator reaches \mark{bottom} sooner or later; when it does not, the saturator may never stop. Is there a machine that can say, for every goal, whether it follows? This topic starts from <part-ref to="lemma:liar"></part-ref> in <level-ref to="kk-one"></level-ref>.
level.u-barber.tasks.u-barber.brief: The village barber says: “I shave exactly those who do not shave themselves.” Given “\(\text{there is an x such that for every y},x\; \text{shaves y}\leftrightarrow y\; \text{does not shave himself}\)”, prove the contradiction \mark{bottom}.
level.u-barber.title: Barber
level.u-cantor.after: This is Cantor’s theorem: a set always has more subsets than elements.
level.u-cantor.tasks.u-cantor.brief: f gives each x a set f(x). Every set is some f(x) (f is onto); and there is a set z holding exactly the y not in f(y). Get the contradiction \mark{bottom}.
level.u-cantor.tasks.u-cantor.hint.0: Take out z first, then the x whose f(x) is z.
level.u-cantor.tasks.u-cantor.hint.1: Taking y = x in both gives \(X\leftrightarrow Y\) and \(Y\leftrightarrow \lnot X\).
level.u-cantor.tasks.u-cantor.hint.2: From these two, build what <part-ref to="lemma:liar"></part-ref> needs.
level.u-cantor.title: Cantor
level.u-halt.after: Passing from one problem to another is a <wiki-ref to="reduction"></wiki-ref>. Provability in first-order logic shows the same <wiki-ref to="undecidable"></wiki-ref>: no program can say, for every goal, whether it follows.
level.u-halt.tasks.u-halt.brief: Given: if some machine decides halting, a machine x can be built that halts on ⟨y⟩ exactly when y does not halt on ⟨y⟩; and if some machine decides A_TM, one deciding halting can be built. Prove no machine decides A_TM.
level.u-halt.tasks.u-halt.hint.0: Assume a machine that decides A_TM.
level.u-halt.tasks.u-halt.hint.1: In the end, a machine still reads its own code.
level.u-halt.title: Halting
level.u-ls.tasks.u-ls.brief: ⟨y⟩ is the code of the Turing machine y. L_s holds the codes of machines that do not accept their own code. Supposing some machine x recognises L_s, get the contradiction \mark{bottom}.
level.u-ls.tasks.u-ls.hint.0: Let x read its own code.
level.u-ls.title: Self rejection
level.x-chain.after: Any box can be traded for K, S and Apply: the <wiki-ref to="deduction"></wiki-ref>.
level.x-chain.tasks.x-chain.hint.0: What does the proof look like with a box? Without one, what does each step inside it?
level.x-chain.tasks.x-chain.hint.1: The Apply inside the box happens under the condition “it rains”.
level.x-chain.title: Chain
level.x-k.intro.0.t: This topic takes the box away, leaving Apply and the K and S you proved. Early provers were like this: one rule, and every other starting point an <wiki-ref to="axiom"></wiki-ref>. Such a prover is a <wiki-ref to="hilbert"></wiki-ref>.
level.x-k.tasks.x-k-2.hint.0: Apply under a condition is what S does.
level.x-k.tasks.x-k-2.hint.1: S’s three sentences need not each be a single word.
level.x-k.tasks.x-k-2.step: Under a condition without a box
level.x-k.title: K and S
level.x-merge.tasks.x-merge.hint.0: Which S can the given go into?
level.x-merge.tasks.x-merge.hint.1: After S is applied to the given, what is still missing? You assembled it in <level-ref to="x-self"></level-ref>.
level.x-merge.title: Merge
level.x-self.tasks.x-self.hint.0: Start from S: what does it give after two Applies?
level.x-self.tasks.x-self.hint.1: S’s second sentence need not be a single word. Both sentences S then needs can be made with K.
level.x-self.title: Identity
level.x-swap.tasks.x-swap.hint.0: Which S can the given go into, and what does Apply then give?
level.x-swap.tasks.x-swap.hint.1: Can K supply the missing part? Once two parts meet end to end, join them as in <level-ref to="x-chain"></level-ref>.
level.x-swap.title: Swap
package.desc: Provides a course on building mathematical proofs with circuits.
package.title: Formal Proof
part.allE.desc: Connect \(\forall x.\, P(x)\) and choose an object \(t\) to obtain \(P(t)\).
part.allE.name: Choose an instance
part.allE.settings.t.label: Which thing
part.allI.desc: Name an arbitrary object \(a\) on the part. Prove \(P(a)\) inside the box and connect it to “Conclusion” to obtain \(\forall x.\, P(x)\) outside. \(a\) must not occur in any open assumption.
part.allI.name: For any
part.allI.regions.0.label: Inside
part.allI.settings.x.label: Name
part.andE.desc: Connect \(A \land B\) to get \(A\) and \(B\) at separate outputs.
part.andE.name: Split
part.andE.revisions.0.desc: Connect \(A \land B\) to get \(A\) and \(B\) at separate outputs. \(A \leftrightarrow B\) means \((A \to B) \land (B \to A)\) and can be split in the same way.
part.andI.name: Join
part.append.desc: Connect the results of different proof routes. Continue with the first route that can still proceed, in numbered order.
part.append.name: Join candidates
part.append.revisions.0.desc: Keep every result that can still proceed, in route order, for later steps to check.
part.append.settings.ways.label: Routes
part.arrow.desc: Two shapes switched on the part: from \(A\to B\), gives \(\lnot A\lor B\); from \(\lnot A\lor B\), gives \(A\to B\).
part.arrow.name: Arrow away
part.arrow.revisions.0.desc: Two shapes switched on the part: from \(A\to B\), gives \(\lnot A\lor B\); from \(\lnot A\lor B\), gives \(A\to B\). Each shape is also a rewrite rule.
part.auto.desc: Searches depth first until done: each step tries Assumption, then Goal apart, then Use a given; a path back to an earlier state is not followed.
part.auto.name: Your own auto (Legacy)
part.axK.desc: Choose two sentences \(A\) and \(B\) on the part; gives \(A \to (B \to A)\).
part.axK.settings.A.label: First
part.axK.settings.B.label: Second
part.axS.desc: Choose three sentences \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) on the part; gives \((A \to (B \to C)) \to ((A \to B) \to (A \to C))\).
part.axS.settings.A.label: First
part.axS.settings.B.label: Second
part.axS.settings.C.label: Third
part.botE.desc: From the contradiction \(\bot\), gives whatever sentence is chosen on the part.
part.botE.name: Explosion
part.botE.settings.C.label: Conclude
part.chain.desc: From \(A \to B\) and \(B \to C\), gives \(A \to C\).
part.chain.name: Chain
part.clausify.desc: Adds the negated goal to the hypotheses, brings them to CNF, removes the existential quantifiers and splits them into clauses.
part.clausify.name: Into clauses, all the way (Legacy)
part.defer.desc: Moves the first goal to the end; the second becomes the first.
part.defer.name: Defer
part.dist.desc: “Or” distributed over “and”, four shapes switched on the part: \(A\lor (B\land C)\) and \((A\lor B)\land (A\lor C)\) give each other, and so do \((A\land B)\lor C\) and \((A\lor C)\land (B\lor C)\).
part.dist.name: Distribute
part.dist.revisions.0.desc: “Or” distributed over “and”, four shapes switched on the part: \(A\lor (B\land C)\) and \((A\lor B)\land (A\lor C)\) give each other, and so do \((A\land B)\lor C\) and \((A\lor C)\land (B\lor C)\). Each shape is also a rewrite rule.
part.dm.desc: A negation trades “or” for “and” and back, four shapes switched on the part: \(\lnot (A\lor B)\) and \(\lnot A\land \lnot B\) give each other, and so do \(\lnot (A\land B)\) and \(\lnot A\lor \lnot B\).
part.dm.name: De Morgan
part.dm.revisions.0.desc: A negation trades “or” for “and”, “there is” for “for all”, and back: eight shapes switched on the part.
part.dneg.desc: Two shapes switched on the part: from \(\lnot \lnot A\), gives \(A\); from \(A\), gives \(\lnot \lnot A\).
part.dneg.name: Double negation
part.dneg.revisions.0.desc: Two shapes switched on the part: from \(\lnot \lnot A\), gives \(A\); from \(A\), gives \(\lnot \lnot A\). Each shape is also a rewrite rule.
part.each.desc: The parts inside run once on each goal, seeing only that goal each time; if any goal fails, the whole part fails.
part.each.name: Each goal
part.each.regions.0.label: Each goal
part.elimRules.desc: Applies every elimination rule to the hypotheses: Split, Case analysis, applying an “if”, Explosion, the instance box, and choose an instance then use it. Each fit gives one result.
part.elimRules.name: Use a given (Legacy)
part.erule.desc: Takes rules: the rule’s conclusion is unified with the first goal and its first premise with one of that goal’s hypotheses; the goal is replaced by the remaining premises, one goal each. Given several rules, it uses the first that applies.
part.erule.name: A rule, then a given (Legacy)
part.erule.revisions.0.desc: Takes rules: the rule’s conclusion is unified with the first goal and its first premise with one of that goal’s hypotheses; the goal is replaced by the remaining premises, one goal each. Each rule wired in, and each hypothesis that fits, gives one result.
part.exE.desc: Connect \(\exists x.\, P(x)\) and name the existing object \(a\) on the part. Inside the box, \(P(a)\) may be assumed. Prove \(C\) and connect it to “Conclusion” to obtain \(C\) outside. \(a\) must not appear in \(C\) or in any open assumption.
part.exE.name: Witness
part.exE.regions.0.label: Inside
part.exE.settings.x.label: Witness
part.exI.desc: Connect \(P(t)\) to obtain \(\exists x.\, P(x)\), with \(t\) as a witness. If exactly one existential statement fits, it is selected automatically; if several fit, choose the conclusion on the part.
part.exI.name: Generalise
part.exI.settings.target.label: Conclusion to derive
part.frule.desc: Takes rules: the rule’s first premise is unified with one of the first goal’s hypotheses and its conclusion is added to the hypotheses; each remaining premise becomes a goal, placed first. Given several rules, it uses the first that applies.
part.frule.name: One step forward (Legacy)
part.gAnd.desc: \(a \land b\): outputs true only when both inputs are true; otherwise false.
part.gAnd.name: And \mark{and}
part.gFalse.desc: Negates the output of Always True. The output is false for every pair of inputs.
part.gFalse.name: Contradiction \mark{bottom}
part.gIff.desc: \(a \leftrightarrow b\): outputs true when \(a\) and \(b\) are both true or both false; false when one is true and the other false.
part.gIff.name: Equivalent \mark{iff}
part.gImp.desc: Outputs false only when \(a\) is true and \(b\) is false; true otherwise.
part.gImp.name: Implies \mark{implies}
part.gNot.desc: \(\lnot a\): true in gives false out; false in gives true out.
part.gNot.name: Not \mark{not}
part.gOr.desc: Outputs true when at least one input is true; false when both are false.
part.gOr.name: Or \mark{or}
part.gTrue.desc: The two directions of Implies joined by Or. The output is true for every pair of inputs.
part.gTrue.name: Always True \mark{top}
part.iff.desc: Two shapes switched on the part: from \(A\leftrightarrow B\), gives \((\lnot A\lor B)\land (\lnot B\lor A)\), and the other way round. Each shape is also a rewrite rule.
part.iff.name: Equivalence away
part.iffSubst.desc: Connect the equivalence and the original sentence. The sentence shows a box around each replaceable subformula. Select one box to replace its contents with the right side of the equivalence.
part.iffSubst.inputs.0.label: Equivalence
part.iffSubst.inputs.1.label: Original sentence
part.iffSubst.name: Eq. substitution
part.impI.desc: A box, with \(A\) set on the part. Inside, \(A\) may be used as an assumption; prove \(B\) there and wire it to “Conclusion”, and the part gives \(A \to B\).
part.impI.name: Assume
part.impI.regions.0.label: Inside
part.impI.settings.A.label: Assume
part.introRules.desc: Applies every introduction rule backwards to the first goal: Join, the assumption box, Add alternative left and right, the for-any box, Generalise. Each rule that fits gives one result.
part.introRules.name: Goal apart (Legacy)
part.lem.desc: Choose a sentence \(A\) on the part; gives \(A \lor \lnot A\).
part.lem.name: Excluded middle
part.liar.name: The liar
part.merge.name: Merge
part.metis.desc: Turns the goal into clauses, finds a certificate that reaches \(\bot\) and has the kernel replay it: if it passes, the goal is closed; if the certificate fails the check, the part fails.
part.metis.name: Reconstructor (Legacy)
part.mp.name: Apply
part.mp.revisions.0.desc: From \(A \to B\) and \(A\), gives \(B\). \(\lnot A\) is \(A \to \bot\), so from \(\lnot A\) and \(A\), gives the contradiction \(\bot\).
part.orE.desc: Connect \(A \lor B\) and assume \(A\) and \(B\) in separate boxes. When both prove the same \(C\) and connect it to their respective “Conclusion” ports, the part outputs \(C\).
part.orE.name: Case analysis
part.orE.regions.0.label: Case one
part.orE.regions.1.label: Case two
part.orI.desc: Connect \(A\) and choose another statement \(B\) and its position to get \(A \lor B\) or \(B \lor A\). \(B\) need not be proved.
part.orI.name: Add alternative
part.orI.settings.other.label: Added disjunct
part.orI.settings.side.label: Position
part.orI.settings.side.options.0.label: Left
part.orI.settings.side.options.1.label: Right
part.oracle.desc: A fast prover: it cancels all complementary literals between two clauses at once, round after round until \(\bot\) appears or no new clause does. It too records the two parents of each new clause.
part.oracle.name: Someone else’s prover
part.raa.name: By contradiction
part.refl.desc: Choose a thing \(t\) on the part; gives \(t = t\).
part.refl.name: Reflexivity
part.refl.settings.t.label: Which thing
part.repeat.desc: The frame receives the input; its inner output goes to “Result” and back into the frame, round after round, until it stops changing, and the last round’s result is given. If a round fails, it stops at the round before.
part.repeat.name: Repeat frame
part.repeat.regions.0.label: Each round
part.repeat.revisions.0.desc: The frame receives the input; its inner output goes to “Result” and back into the frame, round after round, until it stops changing, and the last round’s result is given. If a round fails, it stops at the round before. With several results, it goes on from the first only.
part.replay.desc: When the clause set contains \(\bot\), the steps to \(\bot\) go to the kernel: each input clause used must come from a hypothesis, and each step must be proved from its two parents (variables instantiated by unification) by Own auto. If all pass, the goal the clauses came from is proved; otherwise it names the failing step.
part.replay.name: Replay
part.res.desc: Wire in two clauses, one holding \(A\) and the other \(\lnot A\), in any position: that pair is cancelled and what is left is joined with “or”; when nothing is left, gives the contradiction \(\bot\). One pair at a time.
part.res.name: Resolve
part.resolve.desc: Tries every pair of clauses in the set once: when a literal of one unifies with the complement of a literal of the other, that pair is cancelled and the remaining literals form a new clause, added with a record of its two parents. Tautologies and duplicates are dropped. It can be set to resolve only against one-literal clauses.
part.resolve.name: Resolution round
part.resolve.settings.unit.label: Cancel with
part.rewrite.desc: Wire in \(s = t\) and a sentence containing \(s\); the part marks each \(s\) in it, and the ticked ones become \(t\).
part.rewrite.name: Substitute equals
part.rewrite.settings.at.label: Which occurrences to replace
part.rule.desc: Takes rules at its “R” port and uses the first that applies: the first goal is unified with the rule’s conclusion and replaced by its premises (one goal per premise, each premise’s own assumptions added to the hypotheses). Any ?-letter not yet fixed stays in the goals.
part.rule.name: Apply a rule backwards (Legacy)
part.rw.desc: Takes rewrite rules: in the first goal, outside in and left to right, the first place that fits the rule’s left side becomes its right side, that place alone. A rule with conditions adds each as a new goal after this one. Given several, it uses the first that fits; if nothing fits, it fails.
part.rw.inputs.1.label: Rule
part.rw.name: Rewrite (Legacy)
part.rw.revisions.0.desc: Takes rewrite rules: in the first goal, outside in and left to right, the first place that fits the rule’s left side becomes its right side, that place alone. A rule with conditions adds each as a new goal after this one. Given several, it uses the first that fits; if nothing fits, it fails. With “Where” set to the hypotheses, it rewrites the first goal’s first hypothesis from the top that fits.
part.rw.settings.at.label: Where
part.rw.settings.at.options.0.label: Goal
part.rw.settings.at.options.1.label: Hypotheses
part.saturate.desc: Resolves round after round until \(\bot\) appears or no new clause does.
part.saturate.name: The saturator
part.search.desc: Depth-first search: the parts inside take one step on the state received, then go on from each result; each path is followed to its end before backtracking to the next, until no goal remains. Gives every finished state it finds. A step back to where it was (no fewer goals, no more hypotheses) is not followed. A depth limit can be set on the part.
part.search.name: Backtracking
part.search.regions.0.label: Each step
part.search.settings.depth.label: At most
part.simp.desc: Takes a list of rewrite rules: each round, the first that fits rewrites one place, round after round, until none fits.
part.simp.name: Simp (Legacy)
part.simp.revisions.0.desc: Takes a list of rewrite rules: each round, the first that fits rewrites one place, round after round, until none fits. With “Where” set to the hypotheses, it rewrites the first goal’s hypotheses.
part.simp.settings.at.label: Where
part.simp.settings.at.options.0.label: Goal
part.simp.settings.at.options.1.label: Hypotheses
part.skolem.desc: Removes every \(\exists\) from the first goal’s hypotheses: one with no \(\forall\) outside is taken out as the instance box does; one under a \(\forall\) becomes a new function of all the enclosing \(\forall\) variables (\(sk1(x)\) …). The hypotheses must be in negation normal form first.
part.skolem.name: Skolemise
part.swap.name: Swap
part.toClauses.desc: The first goal must be \(\bot\): its hypotheses are split into clauses. Each must be in CNF; conjunctions are split, each disjunction becomes a clause, universal quantifiers are dropped and variables read as universally quantified.
part.toClauses.name: Extract clauses
